sessions.title: Experiments, atomic outcomes & sample-space audits
sessions.focus: Choose complete mutually exclusive outcome records before event algebra.
sessions.purpose: Make finite probability begin with a defensible model rather than an inherited denominator.
sessions.centralCapability: Define an experiment, construct/audit a finite atomic sample space, and represent events as subsets.
sessions.principalObstacle: The learner lists overlapping labels instead of complete atomic records or assumes the physical story fixes a unique sample space.
requiredOwnership: Define the experiment and atomic outcomes.
Construct a complete finite sample space.
Represent an event as a subset of the sample space.
Distinguish an outcome from an event.
Form event intersection/union from stated conditions.
sessions.applicationScope: Finite probability reasoning on explicitly specified sample spaces and probability models.
sessions.transferScope: Changed-surface transfer: Invalid overlapping label list → learner repairs a common recording rule and atomic representation.
sessions.exitCondition: Model an unfamiliar finite experiment and translate verbal conditions into event subsets.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. Before asking for a probability, decide what one complete outcome record is. A sample space is a model of the experiment, not a bag of interesting words.

Define. An experiment specifies what is done and recorded. An atomic outcome is one complete mutually exclusive record. Ω is the set of all possible atomic outcomes. An event is a subset of Ω, so an event may contain many atoms.

Connect. M03 set notation now gets a probabilistic meaning: union is “A or B”, intersection is “A and B”, complement is “not A”. Ordered pairs from M03 are useful when a record has two components.

Explain. If a coin is tossed and a digit from {1,2,3} is recorded, the atom is not “tail” or “odd”; it is a complete pair such as (T,3). The six pairs are mutually exclusive and exhaustive. A proposed space such as {H,T,odd,even} is invalid because its members overlap and do not represent one common recording rule.

Worked example: A device records channel {L,R} and status {ok,fail}. Use Ω={(L,ok),(L,fail),(R,ok),(R,fail)}. Event C='channel L' contains two atoms; event F='fail' contains two; C∩F={(L,fail)} and C∪F contains three atoms.

Guided check: A spinner records colour {red,blue} and then a switch records {on,off}. Write Ω, the event “blue”, and the event “blue and on”. Then explain why “blue” is not one atomic record.

Fade. On an independent task, first audit whether the proposed outcomes are mutually exclusive, exhaustive and complete records before doing any set algebra.

Distinction check. The same physical situation can support different sample spaces if the experiment records different information. The model is defined by the recording rule.
sessions.guidedFeedback: Check after attempting. Ω has four ordered pairs: (red,on),(red,off),(blue,on),(blue,off). “blue” is the two-atom event {(blue,on),(blue,off)}; “blue and on” is the single atom {(blue,on)}.

sessions.title: Finite probability models, axioms & normalization
sessions.focus: Assigning legal weights to finite outcomes.
sessions.purpose: Separate sample-space structure from probability weights.
sessions.centralCapability: Validate and complete a finite probability model using nonnegativity and total mass 1.
sessions.principalObstacle: Probability is treated as automatically uniform or weights are accepted without normalization.
requiredOwnership: Assign probability to atomic outcomes.
Check nonnegativity.
Check total probability equals 1.
Solve a missing probability by normalization.
Compute an event probability by summing atomic weights.
sessions.applicationScope: Finite probability reasoning on explicitly specified sample spaces and probability models.
sessions.transferScope: Changed-surface transfer: Forward normalization exercise → audit an illegal probability ledger and repair one mass while preserving the others.
sessions.exitCondition: Audit or complete a nonuniform finite model and calculate event probabilities.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. Finite does not mean uniform. Once the atoms are clear, a probability model must say how much mass each atom receives.

Define. Every atomic probability is nonnegative and the total atomic mass is 1. The probability of an event is the sum of the masses of its atoms. Equal mass 1/|Ω| is one legal special case, not the definition.

Connect. From S01 an event is a subset of Ω; from M01/M02 we can sum decimals/fractions and solve a missing value.

Explain. On Ω={r,s,t}, masses .10,.25,.65 form a legal model. Event {r,t} has probability .75. If the last mass were .75 instead, the total would be 1.10, so the assignment would not be a probability model even though each individual number lies between 0 and 1.

Worked example: Ω={a,b,c,d} has masses .18,.27,p,.20. Normalization gives p=.35. Then P({b,c})=.62. A proposed p=.40 fails because the total would be 1.05.

Guided check: Ω={u,v,w} has masses q,.32,.41. Find q, verify legality, and compute P({u,w}).

Fade. Do not “repair” a model by assuming uniformity. Use the stated mass and check both nonnegativity and normalization.

Distinction check. “All probabilities are between 0 and 1” is necessary but not sufficient for a finite atomic assignment; the masses must also total exactly 1.
sessions.guidedFeedback: Check after attempting. q=1-.32-.41=.27; all three masses are nonnegative and total1. P({u,w})=.27+.41=.68.

sessions.title: Equally likely outcomes & counting probability
sessions.focus: Favourable-over-total counts when atomic outcomes truly have equal probability.
sessions.purpose: Connect M03 counting to finite probability without assuming uniformity by default.
sessions.centralCapability: Use counting only after justifying equal atomic probabilities.
sessions.principalObstacle: Favourable/total is used in nonuniform spaces or the denominator counts the wrong atomic outcomes.
requiredOwnership: Justify when atomic outcomes are equally likely.
Count the total atomic outcomes.
Count favourable outcomes.
Compute favourable/total probability.
Reject favourable/total when equiprobability is absent.
sessions.applicationScope: Finite probability reasoning on explicitly specified sample spaces and probability models.
sessions.transferScope: Changed-surface transfer: Atomic fair outcomes → aggregated dashboard labels with unequal multiplicities.
sessions.exitCondition: Solve a counting probability and state why the denominator is legitimate.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. Counting gives probability only after a modeling decision: are the atomic outcomes equally likely?

Define. If N atomic outcomes are equiprobable, each has mass 1/N and P(E)=|E|/N. Aggregated labels need not be equiprobable even when the underlying atoms are.

Connect. M03 supplies product counting and combinations. S02 supplies the probability model that justifies favourable/total.

Explain. Two fair dice have 36 equiprobable ordered pairs, but the eleven possible sums are not equiprobable: sum2 has one pair, sum7 has six. The correct denominator is the atomic pair space, not the number of distinct labels.

Worked example: Choose uniformly from {1,2,3}×{A,B}. Six pairs are equiprobable. Event “number at least2 and letter B” has two atoms, so probability2/6=1/3.

Guided check: A 4-bit string is chosen uniformly. How many atomic strings have exactly one 1? Use the atom count to compute the probability, then explain why the labels “zero ones, one one, two ones, three ones, four ones” are not five equally likely outcomes.

Fade. Before using favourable/total, state what the atoms are and why they have equal mass.

Distinction check. Fair component mechanisms do not imply every derived summary label is equally likely; multiplicity matters.
sessions.guidedFeedback: Check after attempting. Exactly one 1 has four strings, so probability4/16=1/4. The five count labels contain 1,4,6,4,1 atomic strings respectively, so they are not equiprobable.

sessions.title: Complements, certainty, impossibility & at-least-one basics
sessions.focus: Complement rule and boundary events.
sessions.purpose: Make complement reasoning automatic before harder repeated-trial problems.
sessions.centralCapability: Use P(A^c)=1−P(A) and identify certain/impossible events.
sessions.principalObstacle: Complement is confused with 'opposite-looking' wording or at-least-one is counted directly when none is easier.
requiredOwnership: Identify event complement exactly.
Use P(A^c)=1−P(A).
Recognize P(Ω)=1.
Recognize P(∅)=0.
Use a complement to compute an at-least-one event in a finite model.
sessions.applicationScope: Finite probability reasoning on explicitly specified sample spaces and probability models.
sessions.transferScope: Changed-surface transfer: Direct complement calculation → diagnose a linguistically plausible but set-theoretically wrong complement.
sessions.exitCondition: Translate verbal complements exactly and use them to simplify probability calculations.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. “Not A” is an exact set operation, not whichever event sounds like the verbal opposite.

Define. A^c contains precisely the atoms in Ω that are not in A. A and A^c are disjoint and cover Ω, so P(A^c)=1-P(A), P(Ω)=1 and P(∅)=0.

Connect. M03 set complement gives the set identity; S02 turns the disjoint partition into a probability equation.

Explain. If A='at least one success', then A^c='no successes', not 'all failures except some other special case' and not 'all successes'. Complements are defined by membership, not by linguistic symmetry.

Worked example: A uniform spinner has labels1–8. A='multiple of3'={3,6}; A^c={1,2,4,5,7,8}, so P(A^c)=6/8=3/4.

Guided check: A 3-bit string is chosen uniformly. Let B='at least one 1'. Identify B^c and compute P(B) by complement.

Fade. When the target says “at least one”, test whether “none” is a single, easier complement event before enumerating cases.

Distinction check. Certain and impossible events are Ω and ∅. Their probabilities are boundary consequences of the model, not informal confidence statements.
sessions.guidedFeedback: Check after attempting. B^c={000}, so P(B)=1-1/8=7/8.

sessions.title: Union, intersection & the addition rule
sessions.focus: Disjoint and overlapping event combinations.
sessions.purpose: Translate event algebra into probability arithmetic.
sessions.centralCapability: Compute unions/intersections and apply the disjoint addition rule with correct conditions.
sessions.principalObstacle: Probabilities are added blindly even when events overlap.
requiredOwnership: Interpret A∪B and A∩B as events.
Identify whether two events are disjoint.
Use P(A∪B)=P(A)+P(B) for disjoint events.
Explain why overlap causes double counting.
Compute simple union/intersection probabilities from an explicit finite model.
sessions.applicationScope: Finite probability reasoning on explicitly specified sample spaces and probability models.
sessions.transferScope: Changed-surface transfer: Explicit sets → region-count ledger; disjointness and addition must be inferred from the overlap cell.
sessions.exitCondition: Decide whether addition is legal and compute event combinations from a finite model.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. “A or B” in mathematics is inclusive unless stated otherwise; overlap is where naive addition breaks.

Define. A∪B contains atoms in A, B or both. A∩B contains atoms in both. Events are disjoint when A∩B=∅. For disjoint events only, P(A∪B)=P(A)+P(B).

Connect. M03 event-set operations identify the regions; S02 supplies event mass.

Explain. A useful region ledger is: A-only, both, B-only, neither. If the “both” region is empty, adding P(A)+P(B) counts every union atom once. If it is nonempty, direct addition counts that region twice.

Worked example: On a uniform die, A={1,2}, B={5,6}. They are disjoint, so P(A∪B)=2/6+2/6=4/6. With C={2,3}, A∩C={2}; direct addition would double-count2.

Guided check: On Ω={1,...,10} uniformly, E={1,2,3} and F={7,8,9,10}. Decide disjointness and compute P(E∪F). Then change F to {3,7,8,9}; identify exactly what breaks.

Fade. Never choose the addition rule from the word “or” alone; inspect the intersection first.

Distinction check. Disjointness is about impossible co-occurrence. Independence, introduced later, is a different probability property.
sessions.guidedFeedback: Check after attempting. First E∩F=∅ and P(E∪F)=7/10. After changing F, the overlap is {3}; blind addition counts that atom twice.

sessions.title: Two-event inclusion–exclusion in probability
sessions.focus: Correcting overlap in union probabilities.
sessions.purpose: Generalize the addition rule to arbitrary two events.
sessions.centralCapability: Use and justify P(A∪B)=P(A)+P(B)−P(A∩B).
sessions.principalObstacle: Intersection is subtracted with the wrong sign or omitted.
requiredOwnership: State the two-event inclusion-exclusion formula.
Explain the overlap correction.
Solve for a union probability.
Rearrange the formula to recover an intersection.
Check probability bounds/consistency.
sessions.applicationScope: Finite probability reasoning on explicitly specified sample spaces and probability models.
sessions.transferScope: Changed-surface transfer: Forward inclusion–exclusion → infer the missing overlap and neither region from aggregate counts.
sessions.exitCondition: Use inclusion-exclusion forward and backward and detect inconsistent inputs.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. When two events overlap, union probability is a bookkeeping problem: count every union atom exactly once.

Define. P(A∪B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A∩B). The subtraction removes the second copy of the overlap.

Connect. S05 supplied the region ledger. M03 inclusion–exclusion supplied the set-counting analogue.

Explain. The formula can run forward to a union or backward to an intersection. Any recovered intersection must satisfy 0≤P(A∩B)≤min(P(A),P(B)); the union must lie between each marginal and1.

Worked example: P(A)=.42,P(B)=.36,P(A∩B)=.14 gives union .64. If instead union=.64 is known, rearrangement recovers overlap .14.

Guided check: P(C)=.55,P(D)=.30,P(C∪D)=.68. Recover P(C∩D), check its bounds, and find the probability of neither C nor D.

Fade. Use the region meaning to check the sign: overlap is subtracted once, never added as a “correction.”

Distinction check. A numerically computed value outside probability bounds is evidence of a modeling/algebra error, not an exotic probability.
sessions.guidedFeedback: Check after attempting. P(C∩D)=.55+.30-.68=.17, which is between0 and.30. Neither has probability1-.68=.32.

sessions.title: Conditional probability: restricted mass, tables & direction
sessions.focus: Conditioning as reference-population restriction and renormalization, not causal reversal.
sessions.purpose: Make the denominator, direction and information meaning of conditioning visible across atom-ledger and two-way-table representations.
sessions.centralCapability: Interpret and compute finite P(A|B)=P(A∩B)/P(B) for P(B)>0, including nonuniform mass and reverse-direction comparisons.
sessions.principalObstacle: The learner keeps the original denominator, treats favourable/total as universal, reverses the bar, or thinks later information cannot condition an earlier event.
requiredOwnership: Interpret conditioning as restricting to B.
Use P(A|B)=P(A∩B)/P(B).
Use the correct denominator P(B).
Distinguish P(A|B) from P(B|A).
State the P(B)>0 requirement.
sessions.applicationScope: Finite probability models represented as explicit atomic mass ledgers, restricted outcome lists or complete two-way count tables.
sessions.transferScope: Changed-surface transfer: Nonuniform atom ledger → two-way table plus chronological-information misconception.
sessions.exitCondition: Restrict to the conditioning event, renormalize its mass, track direction/denominator, and explain why information timing is not the same as physical causation.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. Two analysts can use the same joint data and get different conditional probabilities because the bar changes the reference population. The question is not “which event caused the other?” but “after I am told B occurred, what probability mass is still eligible?”

Define. For finite events A and B with P(B)>0,
P(A|B)=P(A∩B)/P(B).
Conditioning on B discards outcomes outside B and rescales the mass inside B to total 1. This definition works for unequal atomic probabilities too; favourable-count/total-count is only the special case where the surviving atomic outcomes are equiprobable. Reversing the bar changes the denominator: P(A|B) and P(B|A) generally answer different questions.

Connect. From S02, event probability is the sum of its atomic masses. From S05, A∩B is the part satisfying both conditions. Therefore the conditional numerator is the surviving mass that also satisfies A, and the denominator is all surviving B-mass.

Explain. Suppose Ω={u,v,w,x} with masses .10,.20,.30,.40. Let A={u,x} and B={v,w,x}. Then P(B)=.90 and P(A∩B)=.40, so P(A|B)=.40/.90=4/9. In the reverse direction P(A)=.50, so P(B|A)=.40/.50=4/5. The same overlap .40 appears in both numerators, but the reference populations differ. If P(B)=0, the finite ratio is undefined.

Worked example: A complete count table can encode the same restriction idea:
            F   not F   total
X          12      8      20
not X       3     17      20
total      15     25      40
For P(F|X), keep only the X row: 12 of 20, so 3/5. For P(X|F), keep only the F column: 12 of 15, so 4/5. The table is not a new formula; it is a compact picture of the joint counts and the restricted denominator.

Guided check: A finite model has masses P(a)=.15,P(b)=.25,P(c)=.10,P(d)=.20,P(e)=.30. Let C={b,d,e} and D={a,d,e}. Without counting outcomes, compute P(C|D) and name the exact denominator mass you used. Then say whether P(D|C) must be the same number.

Fade. On an independent task, first identify the conditioning event and its total mass/count before writing any ratio. Do not assume the atoms are uniform unless the model says so.

Distinction check. Information can arrive after the underlying event without “changing the past.” If a sealed record was generated earlier and a later report tells you that the record lies in B, the physical record is unchanged but your reference set is now B. Conditional probability is information restriction, not backward causation.
sessions.guidedFeedback: Check after attempting. D={a,d,e} has mass .15+.20+.30=.65. C∩D={d,e} has mass .50, so P(C|D)=.50/.65=10/13. The reverse uses denominator P(C)=.25+.20+.30=.75, so it need not match.

representations.title: Conditioning changes the reference row or column
representations.note: Read P(F|X) inside the X row; read P(X|F) inside the F column. The overlap cell is the same, but the denominator changes.

sessions.title: Multiplication rule & intersections from conditionals
sessions.focus: Turning conditional probabilities into joint probabilities.
sessions.purpose: Connect restricted-universe reasoning to sequential/joint events.
sessions.centralCapability: Use P(A∩B)=P(B)P(A|B)=P(A)P(B|A).
sessions.principalObstacle: Conditional and joint probabilities are multiplied or compared without tracking which event is the conditioning base.
requiredOwnership: State the multiplication rule.
Compute an intersection from a conditional probability.
Use either ordering consistently.
Recover a conditional from a joint probability.
Check that a joint probability cannot exceed either marginal.
sessions.applicationScope: Finite probability reasoning on explicitly specified sample spaces and probability models.
sessions.transferScope: Changed-surface transfer: Joint-from-conditional execution → diagnose illegal marginal multiplication and repair the model.
sessions.exitCondition: Move correctly between joint and conditional probabilities.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. A conditional probability can be turned into a joint probability, but only if the conditioning base is tracked.

Define. From P(A|B)=P(A∩B)/P(B), for P(B)>0,
P(A∩B)=P(B)P(A|B).
The same joint also equals P(A)P(B|A) when P(A)>0.

Connect. S07 supplied the conditional denominator. The multiplication rule is just that definition rearranged; it is not permission to multiply arbitrary marginals.

Explain. If P(B)=.50 and P(A|B)=.30, the A∩B mass is .15. If P(A)=.60, then P(B|A)=.15/.60=.25. The joint must be no larger than either marginal because A∩B⊆A and A∩B⊆B.

Worked example: P(C)=.40 and P(D|C)=.65 give P(C∩D)=.26. If P(D)=.50, then P(C|D)=.26/.50=.52.

Guided check: P(E)=.70,P(F|E)=.20 and P(F)=.35. Find P(E∩F) and P(E|F). Check the joint against both marginals.

Fade. Before multiplying, say which factor is a marginal and which is a conditional. Multiplying P(A)P(B) is justified only after independence is established.

Distinction check. Joint, conditional and marginal probabilities are different objects even when their numbers occasionally coincide.
sessions.guidedFeedback: Check after attempting. P(E∩F)=.70×.20=.14; P(E|F)=.14/.35=.40. The joint .14 is below both .70 and .35.

sessions.title: Probability trees: branches, paths & marginals
sessions.focus: Construct/read trees, multiply along paths and add disjoint leaves.
sessions.purpose: Make multi-stage conditional structure visible and auditable before general partition algebra.
sessions.centralCapability: Build a probability tree, multiply along paths and add disjoint leaves.
sessions.principalObstacle: Branch conditionals are mistaken for leaf probabilities, or probabilities are added along a path.
requiredOwnership: Construct a correctly labelled two-stage tree.
Ensure outgoing branch probabilities sum to1.
Multiply conditional probabilities along a path.
Add disjoint leaf probabilities for an event.
Check all leaf probabilities sum to1.
sessions.applicationScope: Finite probability reasoning on explicitly specified sample spaces and probability models.
sessions.transferScope: Changed-surface transfer: Construct a correct tree → audit a malformed partially labelled tree and repair a wrong leaf.
sessions.exitCondition: Model and solve a two-stage finite process with a probability tree.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. Multi-stage probability becomes easier to audit when every conditional branch is visible.

Define. A probability tree starts from a state, labels outgoing branches by conditional probabilities that sum to1 at each node, multiplies along a root-to-leaf path, and adds disjoint leaf probabilities for a multi-leaf event.

Connect. S08 supplies path multiplication; S05 supplies addition across disjoint leaves.

Explain. Rendered tree:
Start
├─ L (.60)
│  ├─ success (.50) → leaf .60×.50=.30
│  └─ fail    (.50) → leaf .30
└─ R (.40)
   ├─ success (.25) → leaf .10
   └─ fail    (.75) → leaf .30
The four leaves sum1. Overall success is .30+.10=.40. This is concrete branch marginalization; S18 later generalizes it to arbitrary partitions.

Worked example: A process chooses A with.70 or B with.30. Given A, pass=.80; given B, pass=.40. The four leaves are .56,.14,.12,.18; pass=.68.

Guided check: A source is X with.25 or Y with.75. Conditional alarm rates are.60 and.20. Sketch the four branches, compute leaf masses, and find total alarm.

Fade. A tree is not decoration. Label the branch conditional first, then multiply; do not write unconditional leaf probabilities directly unless you can justify them.

Distinction check. Add across alternative leaves; multiply along one path. Reversing those operations is a common wrong-solver pattern.
sessions.guidedFeedback: Check after attempting. Leaves: X∩alarm=.15, X∩no=.10, Y∩alarm=.15, Y∩no=.60. They sum1 and total alarm=.30.

representations.title: Two-stage probability tree
representations.note: Multiply along one branch-to-leaf path; add disjoint leaves for a multi-leaf event.

sessions.title: Sampling with vs without replacement
sessions.focus: How sampling protocol changes later conditional probabilities.
sessions.purpose: Prevent independence assumptions from being smuggled into sequential draws.
sessions.centralCapability: Compute sequential probabilities under replacement and without replacement.
sessions.principalObstacle: The second-draw denominator/composition is left unchanged even when the first draw removes an item.
requiredOwnership: State how replacement changes the state.
Compute an ordered two-draw probability with replacement.
Compute it without replacement.
Update numerator and denominator after a draw.
Compare the resulting dependence structures qualitatively.
sessions.applicationScope: Finite probability reasoning on explicitly specified sample spaces and probability models.
sessions.transferScope: Changed-surface transfer: Compute two protocols from wording → infer which candidate second-stage branch belongs to which protocol.
sessions.exitCondition: Solve and compare replacement/nonreplacement sampling problems.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. Drawing twice can look like the same tree while the second-stage state is different.

Define. With replacement, the object is returned and the composition resets. Without replacement, the total decreases and the category count may decrease. Therefore later branch probabilities are protocol-dependent conditionals.

Connect. S09 tree branches make the state change visible; S08 supplies path multiplication.

Explain. Bag3 red,2 blue:
with replacement: P(R then B)=(3/5)(2/5)=6/25;
without replacement: after R, 2R/2B remain, so P(R then B)=(3/5)(2/4)=3/10.
The first branch is the same; the second branch changed because the state changed.

Worked example: Box4 good,1 bad. P(good then good) is (4/5)(4/5)=16/25 with replacement but (4/5)(3/4)=3/5 without replacement.

Guided check: A box has5 green and2 yellow. Compute P(yellow then yellow) under both protocols and explicitly write the second-draw denominator.

Fade. Do not memorize “minus one” mechanically: update the remaining total and the relevant category count from the observed first draw.

Distinction check. Dependence here is created by the sampling protocol, not by a mysterious interaction between physical objects.
sessions.guidedFeedback: Check after attempting. With replacement: (2/7)(2/7)=4/49, second denominator7. Without replacement: (2/7)(1/6)=1/21, second denominator6.

sessions.title: Independence via the product rule
sessions.focus: Event independence as factorization of joint probability.
sessions.purpose: Replace vague 'unrelated' intuition with a testable definition.
sessions.centralCapability: Test A and B using P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B).
sessions.principalObstacle: Events are called independent because they look separate or occur in different descriptions.
requiredOwnership: State the product definition of independence.
Compute both sides of the independence test.
Conclude independence or dependence from equality/inequality.
Distinguish definition from causal intuition.
Use product factorization to recompute a joint probability after independence is established.
sessions.applicationScope: Finite probability reasoning on explicitly specified sample spaces and probability models.
sessions.transferScope: Retrieval/fluency on a new instance; the underlying method and representation are already explicit in instruction.
sessions.exitCondition: Test independence numerically and use it only when justified.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. “They seem unrelated” is not a definition of independence.

Define. A and B are independent exactly when P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B). If the probabilities are positive, equivalent conditional forms appear in S12.

Connect. S08 supplies joints; S10 showed a mechanism that can create dependence.

Explain. On two fair dice, A='first die even', B='second die is6'. P(A)=1/2,P(B)=1/6 and P(A∩B)=3/36=1/12=(1/2)(1/6), so the equality establishes independence. The story about “separate dice” may motivate the model, but the mathematical claim is the equality.

Worked example: On a uniform die, E={1,2,3}, F={1,4}. P(E)=1/2,P(F)=1/3,P(E∩F)=1/6, so they are independent even though both concern the same die.

Explain. Complement bridge retained from the historical repair: if A,B are independent, then
P(A∩B^c)=P(A)-P(A∩B)=P(A)-P(A)P(B)=P(A)(1-P(B))=P(A)P(B^c).
So independence with the complement is derived, not assumed.

Guided check: On a uniform die, test C={1,2} and D={2,4,6} using the product criterion.

Fade. Compute the two sides before using the word independent.

Distinction check. Independence is not “different devices,” “no causal link,” or “disjoint.” Those ideas can disagree with the probability criterion.
sessions.guidedFeedback: Check after attempting. P(C)=1/3,P(D)=1/2,P(C∩D)=1/6 and P(C)P(D)=1/6, so the events are independent.

sessions.title: Independence via conditioning; diagnosing dependence
sessions.focus: P(A|B)=P(A) when P(B)>0.
sessions.purpose: Connect product and conditional definitions and expose dependence as probability change.
sessions.centralCapability: Test whether conditioning changes an event probability.
sessions.principalObstacle: A changed conditional probability is overlooked or conditional equality is used when P(B)=0.
requiredOwnership: State the conditional criterion for independence when P(B)>0.
Compare P(A|B) with P(A).
Diagnose dependence from a change.
Relate the conditional criterion to the product rule.
Respect the positive-denominator condition.
sessions.applicationScope: Finite probability reasoning on explicitly specified sample spaces and probability models.
sessions.transferScope: Changed-surface transfer: Sequential without-replacement story → static marginal/joint probability data requiring conditional/product cross-check.
sessions.exitCondition: Diagnose dependence from conditioning and connect both definitions.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. Independence can also be read as invariance: learning B does not change the probability of A.

Define. For P(B)>0, A and B are independent iff P(A|B)=P(A). A changed conditional probability is evidence of dependence.

Connect. S07 supplies conditioning; S11 supplies the product definition. Algebra links the two criteria.

Explain. From a bag2 red,2 blue, draw twice without replacement. P(second red)=(2/4)(1/3)+(2/4)(2/3)=1/2, while P(second red | first red)=1/3. Because the probability changes, the colour events are dependent. The unconditional value was derived from disjoint first-stage branches, not asserted by symmetry.

Worked example: With replacement from the same bag, the second-draw red probability remains1/2 under either first-draw outcome, and P(second red|first red)=1/2, so the events are independent.

Guided check: A population has P(F)=.40,P(G)=.25 and P(F∩G)=.08. Compute P(F|G) and compare with P(F); check the product criterion too.

Fade. The conditional criterion is legal only when the conditioning event has positive probability.

Distinction check. “Conditioning changes nothing” means the numerical probability stays the same—not that no information was received or no event was observed.
sessions.guidedFeedback: Check after attempting. P(F|G)=.08/.25=.32, which differs from .40; product benchmark .40×.25=.10 also differs from joint .08. The events are dependent.

sessions.title: Mutual exclusivity vs independence
sessions.focus: Disjoint events are usually dependent, not independent.
sessions.purpose: Eliminate one of the most common probability category errors.
sessions.centralCapability: Contrast A∩B=∅ with P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B).
sessions.principalObstacle: 'Cannot happen together' is mistaken for 'do not affect each other'.
requiredOwnership: Define mutual exclusivity/disjointness.
Define independence.
Show positive-probability disjoint events cannot be independent.
Handle the zero-probability edge case.
Give or diagnose examples of each relationship.
sessions.applicationScope: Finite probability reasoning on explicitly specified sample spaces and probability models.
sessions.transferScope: Changed-surface transfer: Given disjoint sets → construct a valid independent non-disjoint pair on a different two-die surface.
sessions.exitCondition: Classify event pairs without conflating structural disjointness and probabilistic independence.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. Two events that cannot happen together are usually the opposite of independent when both have positive probability.

Define. Mutually exclusive/disjoint means A∩B=∅. Independent means P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B). If P(A),P(B)>0 and A,B are disjoint, then 0=P(A∩B)<P(A)P(B), so they are dependent.

Connect. S05 owns disjointness; S11 owns independence.

Explain. On a fair die, A={1,2},B={5,6}. They are disjoint, but P(A)P(B)=1/9 while P(A∩B)=0, so they are not independent. The zero-probability edge case matters: ∅ is disjoint from every event and also satisfies P(∅∩B)=0=P(∅)P(B).

Worked example: A card draw event “red” and “black” are disjoint positive-probability events, so knowing red makes black probability0 rather than leaving it unchanged.

Guided check: On a uniform eight-outcome space, let C have2 atoms and D have3 disjoint atoms. Show dependence numerically, then say what changes if C=∅.

Fade. Classify disjointness from set overlap and independence from probability factorization; do not use one label as evidence for the other.

Distinction check. “Cannot co-occur” and “does not affect probability” are different structural statements.
sessions.guidedFeedback: Check after attempting. P(C)=1/4,P(D)=3/8, product3/32>0 while joint0, so dependent. If C=∅, both joint and product are0, so the edge-case pair is independent.

sessions.title: Pairwise vs mutual independence
sessions.focus: Three-event independence and hidden higher-order dependence.
sessions.purpose: Prevent pairwise checks from being overgeneralized.
sessions.centralCapability: Distinguish pairwise factorization from full three-event factorization.
sessions.principalObstacle: Checking all three pairs is assumed to prove mutual independence.
requiredOwnership: Define pairwise independence for three events.
State the additional triple condition for mutual independence.
Verify all pairwise products.
Check the triple intersection.
Construct/diagnose a pairwise-but-not-mutually-independent example.
sessions.applicationScope: Finite probability reasoning on explicitly specified sample spaces and probability models.
sessions.transferScope: Changed-surface transfer: XOR bit construction → four-atom set system with the same higher-order phenomenon in a different representation.
sessions.exitCondition: Audit a three-event independence claim at pair and triple levels.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. Checking every pair is not enough to establish full independence of three events.

Define. A,B,C are pairwise independent when each pair factors. Mutual independence additionally requires P(A∩B∩C)=P(A)P(B)P(C) for three events.

Connect. S11 supplies the pair criterion; M03 logic warns that several pairwise statements do not automatically imply a stronger collective statement.

Explain. Three independent coin-toss head events have marginals1/2, every pair intersection1/4 and triple1/8, so all required conditions hold. Pairwise checks alone leave the triple unresolved.

Worked example: A simple dependent pair on one die, E='even' and F='>3', already fails the first level because joint2/6 differs from1/4. This contrasts ordinary dependence with the subtler pairwise-but-not-mutual phenomenon left for assessment.

Guided check: State the four equalities that must be checked to establish mutual independence of three positive-probability events.

Fade. Do not stop after the three pair equations when the claim says the three events are mutually independent.

Distinction check. Pairwise independence is genuinely weaker; the missing information lives in a higher-order intersection.
sessions.guidedFeedback: Check after attempting. Check AB, AC and BC factorization, plus P(A∩B∩C)=P(A)P(B)P(C). Pairwise success alone does not settle the fourth equality.

sessions.title: Exact independent paths & randomness fallacies
sessions.focus: Exact sequence probability under constant-p independence, including representativeness and gambler's-fallacy contrasts.
sessions.purpose: Build repeated-trial path probability while separating the mathematical model from visual 'randomness' heuristics.
sessions.centralCapability: Multiply p and 1−p across an exact independent sequence.
sessions.principalObstacle: The learner treats mixed-looking sequences as more likely or expects a run to make the opposite outcome due.
requiredOwnership: Identify repeated identical independent trials.
Assign success probability p and failure1−p.
Compute an exact ordered path probability.
Count powers by number of successes/failures.
Explain why a different ordering has the same probability when p is constant.
sessions.applicationScope: Finite probability reasoning on explicitly specified sample spaces and probability models.
sessions.transferScope: Changed-surface transfer: Direct exact paths → audit a written representativeness/gambler's-fallacy explanation.
inScope: Repeated Bernoulli-style finite trials without distribution naming
sessions.exitCondition: Compute exact ordered success/failure path probabilities and justify the multiplication.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. Randomness does not mean “alternating-looking,” and a run does not make the opposite outcome due.

Define. In repeated independent trials with constant success probability p, an exact ordered path with s successes and f failures has probability p^s(1-p)^f. Order changes the event identity but not the probability when the counts s,f are the same.

Connect. S11 supplies independence factorization; S09 supplies multiplication along a path.

Explain. With p=.60, SSFS and FSSS are different exact events but each has probability .6^3·.4=.0864. A path like SSSS is not “less random” because it contains a run; its probability is computed from the same model. Also, after three successes, the next-trial success probability is still .60 if independence/constant p remains the model.

Worked example: A fair coin has P(HHTHT)=P(HTHTH)=1/32. One sequence looks more alternating, but exact-sequence appearance does not change its probability.

Guided check: Independent trials have p=.70. Compare SSSF and SFSS exactly, then compute P(success on the next trial | first three were successes).

Fade. Separate two questions: the probability of one exact sequence, and the probability of a family of sequences. S16 handles the family count.

Distinction check. Representativeness (“more mixed looks more random”) and the gambler's fallacy (“failure is due”) are not consequences of independence; they predict answers the model rejects.
sessions.guidedFeedback: Check after attempting. Both four-trial paths have probability .7^3·.3=.1029. Under the stated independent constant-p model, P(next success | SSS)=.70, not something smaller because of the run.

sessions.title: Exactly-k successes via combinations
sessions.focus: Counting all ordered paths with k successes.
sessions.purpose: Derive the familiar exactly-k finite-trial formula from M03 combinations plus M04 path probabilities.
sessions.centralCapability: Compute C(n,k)p^k(1−p)^(n−k) without treating it as a memorized distribution formula.
sessions.principalObstacle: The path probability is computed but the number of placements is omitted or multiplied twice.
requiredOwnership: Count success-position choices with C(n,k).
Compute one path probability p^k(1−p)^(n−k).
Multiply count by path probability.
Explain why the paths are disjoint and equally probable.
Avoid naming/using unintroduced distribution machinery.
sessions.applicationScope: Finite probability reasoning on explicitly specified sample spaces and probability models.
sessions.transferScope: Changed-surface transfer: Derive exactly-k correctly → repair a one-path-only solution that omits arrangement count.
sessions.exitCondition: Derive and apply exactly-k success probability from first principles.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. “Exactly k successes” is not one path; it is a disjoint family of paths.

Define. Choose which k of n positions are successes: C(n,k). Every such path has probability p^k(1-p)^(n-k) under independent constant-p trials. Therefore the total is count × one-path probability.

Connect. S15 supplies the path probability; M03-S26 supplies combinations.

Explain. For n=4,p=1/2, exactly two successes has C(4,2)=6 paths, each 1/16, so total6/16=3/8. The coefficient counts placements; it is not an unexplained distribution formula.

Worked example: n=3,p=.40, exactly one success has3 placements and one-path probability .4·.6^2=.144, so total .432.

Guided check: Five independent trials have p=.30. Derive P(exactly two successes) by writing the number of placements and the probability of one representative path.

Fade. If a solver writes only p^k(1-p)^(n-k), ask: “Which arrangements did you count?”

Distinction check. The paths are distinct and disjoint; equal probability lets us multiply one path mass by the number of paths.
sessions.guidedFeedback: Check after attempting. C(5,2)=10 and one path has .3^2·.7^3=.03087, so total .3087.

sessions.title: Complement strategy for none / at least one / all
sessions.focus: Repeated-trial complements.
sessions.purpose: Make 'at least one' calculations efficient and transparent.
sessions.centralCapability: Use P(at least one)=1−P(none) under independent repeated trials.
sessions.principalObstacle: Many overlapping cases are added directly or independence is omitted when computing none/all.
requiredOwnership: Translate at-least-one to the complement of none.
Compute none under independence.
Compute all under independence.
Use the complement rule to get at least one.
Compare direct case counting versus complement efficiency.
sessions.applicationScope: Finite probability reasoning on explicitly specified sample spaces and probability models.
sessions.transferScope: Changed-surface transfer: Choose complement route → diagnose an impossible blind-addition result and separate overlap from complement.
sessions.exitCondition: Choose the complement route for none/at-least-one/all events and justify each factor.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. “At least one” often contains many overlapping stories but has one simple complement.

Define. For n independent trials with success probability p: none=(1-p)^n, all=p^n, and at least one=1-(1-p)^n.

Connect. S04 supplies complements; S15 supplies exact independent path products.

Explain. The complement route is efficient because “none” is one exact path. Summing “success on trial1 or trial2 or …” directly is dangerous because those events overlap. Summing the disjoint exact-count cases from S16 is legal but often longer.

Worked example: Three independent alarms trigger with p=.10. None=.9^3=.729, so at least one=.271; all=.001.

Guided check: Four independent messages are delivered with p=.80. Find none, at least one and all. Then say where independence entered the calculation.

Fade. On a new task, choose a complement only when it genuinely turns the target into a simpler event; do not invoke it by keyword.

Distinction check. Complement logic itself does not require independence. Independence is required here to turn the probability of “none” or “all” into a product of trial probabilities.
sessions.guidedFeedback: Check after attempting. None=.2^4=.0016; at least one=.9984; all=.8^4=.4096. Independence is used in multiplying the four per-trial probabilities.

sessions.title: Partitions, weighted branches & the law of total probability
sessions.focus: General forward marginalization across a finite disjoint exhaustive partition.
sessions.purpose: Generalize concrete tree-leaf addition into a representation-linked law while blocking unweighted averaging and Bayes reversal.
sessions.centralCapability: Compute P(A)=ΣP(B_i)P(A|B_i) over a finite partition.
sessions.principalObstacle: Conditional rates are averaged without branch weights or the forward marginal is mistaken for a reverse conditional.
entryPrerequisites: M03-S17 set operations; JIT disjoint/exhaustive partition definition in this lesson
requiredOwnership: Identify a finite partition.
Verify partition events are disjoint and exhaustive.
Compute branch joint probabilities.
Sum branch contributions to a target event.
State the finite law of total probability without posterior inversion.
sessions.applicationScope: Finite probability reasoning on explicitly specified sample spaces and probability models.
sessions.transferScope: Changed-surface transfer: Build weighted total → audit unweighted rate averaging and an illegal conditional reversal.
sessions.exitCondition: Compute a forward marginal probability by partitioning the sample space.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. Overall rates are weighted by how often each branch occurs. A simple average of subgroup rates is usually wrong when subgroup sizes differ.

Define. A finite partition B1,...,Bk is disjoint and exhaustive. Because A is split into the disjoint pieces A∩Bi,
P(A)=Σ P(Bi)P(A|Bi).
This is the law of total probability: a forward marginalization rule.

Connect. S09 already added disjoint tree leaves for a two-branch case; S08 supplies each joint contribution P(Bi)P(A|Bi). Here we generalize the pattern and connect three representations.

Explain. Contribution table:
branch       P(Bi)   P(error|Bi)   joint contribution
source1      .70         .02             .014
source2      .30         .05             .015
overall error                              .029
A simple average (.02+.05)/2=.035 ignores that source1 occurs more often. The same information can be drawn as a tree; the algebra is the sum of the error leaves.

Worked example: Weekday=.80, weekend=.20; purchase rates .10,.25. Contributions .08 and .05 give overall purchase .13. This computes P(purchase), not P(weekend|purchase).

Guided check: A request is class A=.20,B=.50,C=.30 with escalation rates .40,.10,.25. Compute the three joint contributions and overall escalation. Compare with the unweighted average of the three rates.

Fade. Before summing conditional rates, attach each rate to its branch probability. If the question asks “which branch given the outcome?”, stop: that reverse question belongs to M06 unless a complete joint table already supplies it directly.

Distinction check. Total probability moves from branch probabilities/conditionals to an overall marginal. It is not Bayes' rule.
sessions.guidedFeedback: Check after attempting. Contributions are .08,.05,.075, totaling .205. The unweighted average (.40+.10+.25)/3=.25 is different because the branch shares are unequal.

representations.title: Partition contributions
representations.note: The overall rate is a weighted sum of branch rates, not the unweighted mean of the conditional rates.

sessions.title: Finite expectation as a probability-weighted average
sessions.focus: Expected numerical payoff on a finite probability model.
sessions.purpose: Introduce expectation before decision theory or formal random-variable distributions.
sessions.centralCapability: Compute E[X]=Σx(ω)P(ω) for a finite numerical function/payoff.
sessions.principalObstacle: Expected value is confused with probability, guaranteed payoff or the most likely payoff.
requiredOwnership: Associate a numerical payoff/value with each outcome.
Multiply each value by its probability.
Sum the weighted values.
Check probabilities form a valid model.
Interpret expectation as a probability-weighted average, not a guaranteed outcome.
sessions.applicationScope: Finite probability reasoning on explicitly specified sample spaces and probability models.
sessions.transferScope: Changed-surface transfer: Outcome-value prose → four-leaf payoff table with repeated value labels.
outOfScope: Formal random-variable distribution language until M26
sessions.exitCondition: Compute and interpret a finite expectation from a probability table.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. Probability can weight numerical consequences, not just yes/no events.

Define. For a finite model and numerical value X(ω),
E[X]=Σ X(ω)P(ω).
Expectation is a probability-weighted average. It need not be an attainable outcome and is not a guarantee.

Connect. S02 supplies atomic probability mass; M02 supplies finite sums.

Explain. Values −2,1,5 with probabilities .25,.50,.25 give E[X]=−.50+.50+1.25=1.25. The number1.25 never occurs as a payoff, which is perfectly legal.

Worked example: A score is0 with.50,4 with.30,10 with.20. The model normalizes and E=0+.1.2+2=3.2.

Guided check: Values −1,2,8 occur with probabilities .20,.50,.30. Verify the model and compute the expectation term by term.

Fade. Write value × probability terms before adding; do not average values unless the atoms are equally likely.

Distinction check. Expectation has units of the numerical value, not units of probability. A high-probability outcome and a high expected value are different concepts.
sessions.guidedFeedback: Check after attempting. Probabilities total1. E=(-1)(.2)+2(.5)+8(.3)=-.2+1+2.4=3.2.

sessions.title: Expectation under equally likely finite outcomes & symmetry
sessions.focus: Arithmetic mean of values under uniform atomic probability.
sessions.purpose: Connect uniform probability and symmetry to efficient expectation calculation.
sessions.centralCapability: Use equal weights to average values and exploit balanced pairing when justified.
sessions.principalObstacle: The arithmetic mean is used even when outcomes are not equally likely.
requiredOwnership: Recognize when expectation reduces to an arithmetic mean.
Compute the mean over equally likely atomic outcomes.
Use symmetry/pairing to simplify a finite mean.
Explain why repeated value labels still need atomic multiplicity.
Reject simple averaging for nonuniform probabilities.
sessions.applicationScope: Finite probability reasoning on explicitly specified sample spaces and probability models.
sessions.transferScope: Retrieval/fluency on a new instance; the underlying method and representation are already explicit in instruction.
sessions.exitCondition: Compute uniform finite expectation efficiently and know when simple averaging is invalid.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. Equal atomic probabilities let expectation simplify to an arithmetic mean, but multiplicity still belongs to the atoms.

Define. If N atoms are equally likely, E[X]=(1/N)ΣX(ω). Symmetry can simplify the sum. Averaging distinct value labels is valid only when those labels carry equal total probability.

Connect. S03 distinguishes atoms from aggregated labels; S19 supplies expectation.

Explain. A fair die averages1,...,6 to3.5. Pair1 with6,2 with5,3 with4: each pair sums7, making the symmetry visible. If values repeat on different atoms, repeat them in the atomic average.

Worked example: Uniform values {2,6,10,14} pair to16, so expectation8.

Guided check: Eight equally likely atoms have values {0,0,0,4,4,8,8,8}. Compute the atomic mean. Then compare it with the naive mean of the distinct labels {0,4,8}.

Fade. Ask “equal probability of what?” before replacing a weighted sum with an ordinary mean.

Distinction check. A value label can inherit more mass simply because more atomic outcomes map to it.
sessions.guidedFeedback: Check after attempting. Atomic mean=(0+0+0+4+4+8+8+8)/8=4. The distinct-label mean is also4 here by coincidence; equal numerical results do not make the methods generally interchangeable.

sessions.title: Linearity of expectation
sessions.focus: E[aX+bY+c]=aE[X]+bE[Y]+c without independence.
sessions.purpose: Make expectation algebra powerful before later distribution theory.
sessions.centralCapability: Use finite-sum algebra to prove/apply linearity and explicitly avoid an independence requirement.
sessions.principalObstacle: Linearity is incorrectly restricted to independent quantities or confused with multiplicativity.
requiredOwnership: State linearity for finite expectations.
Derive it from finite weighted sums.
Apply it to aX+bY+c.
Explain independence is not required.
Reject extending linearity to nonlinear operations such as squaring.
sessions.applicationScope: Finite probability reasoning on explicitly specified sample spaces and probability models.
sessions.transferScope: Changed-surface transfer: Explicit outcome proof/application → expectation-only summary data where linearity is usable but nonlinear moments are not recoverable.
sessions.exitCondition: Use and justify linearity on dependent finite quantities.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. Expectation distributes over finite sums even when the underlying quantities are dependent.

Define. E[aX+bY+c]=aE[X]+bE[Y]+c. The proof is finite algebra:
Σ(aX(ω)+bY(ω)+c)P(ω)
=aΣX(ω)P(ω)+bΣY(ω)P(ω)+cΣP(ω).

Connect. S19 supplies the weighted-sum definition; normalization gives ΣP(ω)=1.

Explain. Independence never appears in this derivation. Linearity applies to sums/scalar multiples, not arbitrary nonlinear operations.

Worked example: On two equally likely atoms, X=(0,2),Y=(1,3). E[X]=1,E[Y]=2. Then E[2X-Y+5]=2·1-2+5=5; direct combined values4,6 also average5. But E[X²]=2 while(E[X])²=1.

Guided check: If E[U]=3,E[V]=-1, compute E[4U+2V-7]. State whether dependence matters, then say whether E[U²] follows from E[U] alone.

Fade. Use linearity when the target is an affine combination. Do not “push expectation through” multiplication, squaring or other nonlinear functions without a separate theorem.

Distinction check. Dependence affects many joint quantities, but it does not block finite linearity of expectation.
sessions.guidedFeedback: Check after attempting. E[4U+2V-7]=12-2-7=3. Dependence is irrelevant for this affine expectation; E[U²] is not determined by E[U] alone.

sessions.title: Indicators & expected counts without independence
sessions.focus: I_A and counting by sums of 0/1 variables.
sessions.purpose: Turn difficult expected counts into sums of simple event probabilities.
sessions.centralCapability: Use E[I_A]=P(A) and linearity to count expected occurrences even under dependence.
sessions.principalObstacle: Independence is assumed unnecessarily because the indicator events interact.
requiredOwnership: Define an indicator as 1 on an event and0 otherwise.
Show E[I_A]=P(A).
Represent a count as a sum of indicators.
Use linearity to compute expected count.
Explain independence is unnecessary for the expectation sum.
sessions.applicationScope: Finite probability reasoning on explicitly specified sample spaces and probability models.
sessions.transferScope: Retrieval/fluency on a new instance; the underlying method and representation are already explicit in instruction.
sessions.exitCondition: Compute an expected finite count using indicators under dependent sampling.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. Expected counts can often be computed without enumerating the full joint distribution.

Define. For event A, indicator I_A is1 if A occurs and0 otherwise, so E[I_A]=P(A). If N=I1+...+Ik counts occurrences, linearity gives E[N]=ΣE[Ii]=ΣP(event_i), even when the indicators are dependent.

Connect. S21 supplies linearity. For sampling without replacement, a fixed draw position has the original category fraction because labelled ordered samples place each original object equally often in that position.

Explain. Bag3 red,2 blue; two draws without replacement. For either position, P(red)=3/5 by the labelled-position argument. If I1,I2 indicate red, E[number red]=3/5+3/5=6/5 although the two indicators are dependent.

Worked example: A 2-person committee is chosen uniformly from4 people, two of whom are specialists. Each named specialist has selection probability2/4=1/2, so expected specialists=1.

Guided check: Choose3 of8 people uniformly, where two named people are auditors. Define indicators for each auditor and compute the expected number selected.

Fade. Linearity lets you add expected indicators; it does not assert that the selection events are independent.

Distinction check. Dependence changes joint probabilities, not the identity E[I1+...+Ik]=ΣE[Ii].
sessions.guidedFeedback: Check after attempting. Each named auditor is selected with probability3/8. The count J1+J2 therefore has expectation3/8+3/8=3/4.

sessions.title: Expectation is not most likely, guaranteed or a decision rule
sessions.focus: Interpretation limits of expected value.
sessions.purpose: Prevent expectation from becoming an automatic choice heuristic before M05.
sessions.centralCapability: Separate expectation from modal outcome, attainable outcome, guarantee and decision preference.
sessions.principalObstacle: The largest expectation is treated as synonymous with safest, most likely or universally preferable.
requiredOwnership: Compute a finite expectation.
Identify the most likely outcome separately.
Determine whether the expectation is attainable.
Distinguish expectation from a guarantee.
State that expectation alone does not encode risk preference or choose a decision.
sessions.applicationScope: Finite probability reasoning on explicitly specified sample spaces and probability models.
sessions.transferScope: Changed-surface transfer: Direct model comparison → audit an overreaching decision memo from equal expectation.
sessions.exitCondition: Interpret an expectation without overclaiming what it predicts or recommends.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. Expectation is one summary of a probability model, not a universal decision command.

Define. Expected value may differ from the most likely outcome, may be unattainable, and is not guaranteed. Two models can share an expectation while having very different outcome spreads.

Connect. S19–S22 supplied computation; M05 will later introduce explicit decision/risk criteria.

Explain. Model A pays0 or10 with equal probability, E=5. Model B pays5 for sure, E=5. Equal expectation does not make the models identical and does not determine a universal preference.

Worked example: A payoff is1 with.90 and31 with.10. Expectation4, but the most likely payoff is1 and4 is unattainable.

Guided check: Compare X:0 with.75 or12 with.25 versus Y:3 for sure. Compute expectations, modal outcomes and guarantees before saying what expectation alone can or cannot decide.

Fade. Keep descriptive probability facts separate from a decision rule unless preferences/constraints are explicitly supplied.

Distinction check. “Higher expected value,” “safer,” “more likely to win,” and “better for every decision-maker” are four different claims. M04 owns only the finite probability/expectation facts.
sessions.guidedFeedback: Check after attempting. Both expectations are3. X most often pays0 and guarantees nothing above0; Y always pays3. Equal expectation alone does not choose between them.

sessions.title: M04 synthesis — choose the probability model
sessions.focus: Integrated finite-probability modeling with learner-chosen representation and method.
sessions.purpose: Test whether the learner can organize conditioning, marginalization, dependence and expectation without a supplied formula pipeline.
sessions.centralCapability: Build a finite staged model, compute conditional/joint/marginal probabilities, diagnose dependence and calculate expectation.
sessions.principalObstacle: The learner follows a memorized recipe or infers a posterior/decision conclusion not supported by the givens.
requiredOwnership: Construct the finite staged probability model.
Compute a joint probability from conditionals.
Compute a marginal by total probability.
Diagnose independence from conditional/marginal comparison.
Compute the expectation of a numerical outcome on the resulting leaves.
sessions.applicationScope: Finite probability reasoning on explicitly specified sample spaces and probability models.
sessions.transferScope: Changed-surface transfer: Construct a model → audit another solver's unweighted marginal, independence, expectation and conditional-direction errors.
sessions.exitCondition: Solve a multi-step finite uncertainty problem and defend each selected rule.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. Real probability problems rarely announce which formula should be used. The final skill is to construct an auditable model and choose representations that expose the needed quantities.

Define. A synthesis solution should identify the atoms/branches or table cells, distinguish joint/conditional/marginal quantities, justify any independence claim, and attach numerical values only after the probability model is coherent.

Connect. S07–S18 supply conditioning, trees, independence and total probability; S19–S23 supply expectation. No Bayes inversion or decision theory is needed.

Explain. A useful workflow is not a mandatory recipe: first ask what is given and what is being requested; choose a list, table, tree or algebraic partition that makes the information visible; then apply only relationships whose hypotheses are established. An answer should make its representation and denominator choices inspectable.

Worked example: A shipment comes North=.20/South=.80; damage rates .10/.30. A tree gives damage leaves .02,.24, overall .26. Because .10 differs from .26, source and damage are dependent. With value -5 for damage and +1 otherwise, E=-5(.26)+1(.74)=-.56. No posterior source|damage was computed.

Guided check: Mode L=.30/R=.70; alarm rates .20/.40; value2 for alarm and0 otherwise. Choose either a tree or partition table, find overall alarm, test mode/alarm independence, and compute expectation.

Fade. In independent synthesis, no representation or method is named for you. Make the model choice explicit and let the requested quantities determine the calculations.

Distinction check. A complete solution may legitimately stop when asked for an unavailable reverse conditional or decision preference. Refusing unsupported inference is part of correct modeling.
